operations.new: 1.1 For $n$ large enough that $t_n:=(n/(2\log n))^{1/d}\ge2$, put $m_n=\lfloor t_n\rfloor$ and partition each coordinate interval of $\Omega$ into $m_n$ equal half-open intervals, closing the last interval at its right endpoint. This gives $m_n^d$ disjoint cells covering $\Omega$. Each cell differs from a half-open box with the same coordinate bounds only on its boundary faces, which lie in finitely many coordinate hyperplanes. By [F4] those hyperplanes and every subset of their union are measurable and null, so each cell is measurable and has the same measure as that half-open box, namely $(L/m_n)^d$ by [F1]. The same argument for the boundary of $\Omega$ gives $\lambda_d(\Omega)=L^d$. Hence normalized Lebesgue measure assigns each cell probability $(L/m_n)^d/L^d=m_n^{-d}$. [given, A1, F1, F4, construct]

operations.new: 3.1 Write $\Omega=v+Q[0,L]^d$ using its side length $L>0$ and an orthogonal matrix $Q$, and put $u_i=Q^{\mathsf T}(x_i-v)$. The affine map $F(u)=v+Qu$ bijects the product cube $C_0=[0,L]^d$ onto $\Omega$. For every Borel $E\subseteq C_0$, [F7] gives $\mathbb P(u_i\in E)=\lambda_d(F(E))/\lambda_d(\Omega)=|\det Q|\lambda_d(E)/(|\det Q|\lambda_d(C_0))=\lambda_d(E)/\lambda_d(C_0)$. The transformed samples remain independent: for finitely many Borel sets $E_i\subseteq C_0$, their joint event is $\bigcap_i\{x_i\in F(E_i)\}$, and independence of the $x_i$ makes its probability the product of the individual probabilities. These events are measurable since $F$ is a homeomorphism. Also $\|F(u)-F(w)\|_2=\|u-w\|_2$, so the fill distance of $\{u_1,\ldots,u_n\}$ in $C_0$ equals $h_{X_n}$ in $\Omega$. By [F5], on an event of probability at least $1-1/n$, the fill distance $h_{X_n}$ is at most $\bar h_n=C_dL(\log n/n)^{1/d}$. For all sufficiently large $n$, $\bar h_n<\min(h_0,e^{-1})$; the function $u\mapsto|\log u|/u$ is decreasing on $(0,e^{-1}]$, so [F4] applies and gives $$\sup_xP_{X_n}(x)\le C\exp\!\left(-c\frac{|\log h_{X_n}|}{h_{X_n}}\right) \le C\exp\!\left(-\frac{c}{\bar h_n}\right) =C\exp\!\left(-\frac{c}{C_dL}\left(\frac{n}{\log n}\right)^{1/d}\right).$$ Using this bound in step 2.1 proves the displayed estimate with $A=C$ and $B=c/(C_dL)$, uniformly for every interpolant on that event. [given, A1, F4, F5, F7, step 2.1, algebra] ∎
